newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak central bank warns on economic overheating.
newsitem.headline: Slovak central bank warns on economic overheating.

text.p: Slovakia faces the risk of an overheated economy as a result of rapid growth fuelled by domestic demand, Elena Kohutikova, head of the National Bank of Slovakia's monetary policy department, said on Monday.
"We can already see certain signs of an overheated economy resulting mainly from the speed and the quality of the growth of GDP," she told a seminar on an OECD survey on Slovakia.
Kohutikova said growth of the country's gross domestic product (GDP) was fuelled mainly by domestic demand, which she termed "an unfavourable development from the long-term perspective."
She went on: "From a long-term perspective such a fast increase in domestic demand in an open economy such as Slovakia's, will not be favourable for development."
She would not disclose which steps, if any, the NBS would take to help prevent further overheating of the economy.
Slovakia's GDP rose a real 7.1 percent in the first half of this year. Full year 1995 GDP grew by 7.4 percent.
Domestic demand, which was at the heart of the growth, rose by 23 percent in the first half of this year. The government has forecast GDP growth of at least six percent next year.
The NBS implemented a series of measures in July to tighten the money supply and curb inflation and expansion of credit.

The moves included increases in the last-resort lending facility, the Lombard rate and minimum reserve requirements for banks, which, together with a new NBS measure aimed at curbing domestic lending, gradually boosted interbank money market rates to around 15 percent.
Slovakia's inflation, still one of the lowest in central and eastern Europe, rose 0.7 percent in October, putting the prices 5.3 percent higher year-on-year.
But Slovakia's key money supply measure, M2, rose 19.0 percent year-on-year in September, compared with a 19.5 percent rise in August.
The NBS has stated a 1996 full-year target for M2 expansion of 11.6 percent year-on-year.
